stem:
Anya writes the up-and-down sum $1+2+\cdots+n+\cdots+2+1$ with consecutive counting numbers that climb from $1$ to $n$ and then fall back to $1$.

Why does that sum equal $n^{2}$?

options.text: The sum equals $n^{2}$ for any climb-and-fall of whole numbers, even if the steps are not the consecutive counting numbers from $1$ to $n$ and back.
Say that $n^{2}$ is what produces the up-and-down counting sum, instead of arranging the sum to fill an $n$-by-$n$ square.
The climb from $1$ to $n$ and the fall back to $1$ can be paired to fill an $n$-by-$n$ square of unit tiles, so the sum is $n^{2}$.
The same story also forces triangular and hexagonal number identities, so those must equal $n^{2}$ too.

teacher.key_rationale: The consecutive up-and-down counting sum fills an n-by-n square, so it equals n². Skipping the consecutive-from-1 condition, reversing cause, or dragging in triangular/hexagonal identities miss this hinge.
